tasks.task_description: Build the ball-passing network for the Huskies (players as nodes, passes as links) and characterize its structural and dynamic features across multiple scales: micro (dyadic/triadic pair patterns), meso (position-layer structure, formations), and macro (all 30 players, whole season), and across time from minute-to-minute to the full season.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) a pass is a directed edge origin->destination; the internal Huskies subgraph uses only passes between two Huskies players (cross-team passes are treated as out-edges and excluded from the structural graph but kept for possession share). (ii) Player identity is the 'TeamID_Position#' string; 30 distinct Huskies players appear (G1, D1-D10, M1-M3, F1-F3 plus others), consistent with the stated 30. (iii) Coordinates are in normalized [0,100] attacking-team frame, so 'forward' means destination_x - origin_x > +5 field units and 'backward' < -5; |dx|<=5 is 'sideways'. (iv) Time is reconstructed as EventTime for 1H and EventTime + 2700 s for 2H. (v) The dataset contains no explicit pass-completion flag, so completion is not used as a primary indicator; instead observable pass direction, length, type, and frequency are used. Data cleaning: 23,429 passing rows loaded; 0 rows dropped for missing player IDs, 0 for bad coordinates; whitespace stripped from all string columns; coordinates coerced to numeric. 10,451 of the 23,429 passes are Huskies-internal or Huskies-origin; 59,271 full events, 320 Huskies shots, 500 opponent shots. Method: a weighted directed graph (weight = pass length) with an undirected 0/1 adjacency for topological metrics; dyads from ordered-pair counts, triads from directed 3-paths; degree, clustering, assortativity, and betweenness centrality computed with networkx. This is sound because the question is structural (who passes to whom, how often) and the network is the natural object.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Nodes V = Huskies players (n=30). Directed edge weight W_ij = sum of pass lengths i->j over the season; undirected adjacency A_ij = 1 if W_ij+W_ji > 0. Metrics: density = |E|/(n(n-1)) = 352/435 = 0.810; degree d_i = sum_j A_ij (mean 23.5, max 30, std 5.9); average local clustering C = (1/n) sum_i 2L_i/(d_i(d_i-1)) = 0.935; degree assortativity r = -0.242; betweenness centrality via shortest-path counts. Dyad frequency f_ij = count of i->j passes; top dyads: M1->F2 (182), M3->M1 (168), M1->M3 (143), D3->G1 (120), F2->M1 (117), D1->G1 (107). Triad frequency g_ijk = count of directed 3-paths i->j->k; the dominant triads all route through M1->F2: {M3,D1,D2,G1,M2,D3}->M1->F2 (182 each). Direction split (season): forward 42.3%, backward 24.9%, sideways 32.8%; mean pass length 23.95 field units. Position-layer pass share: D 42.5%, M 37.0%, F 15.9%, G 4.5%. Time-resolved forward-pass fraction by 15-min window: 0-15: 38.8%, 15-30: 41.8%, 30-45: 42.2%, 45-60: 42.4%, 60-75: 41.6%, 75-90: 42.9% (i.e. no strong monotone late-game shift in the aggregate; the shift is outcome-conditional, see Task 3).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The Huskies' passing network is dense (0.81) and highly clustered (0.93) — a tight, interlocking core rather than a sparse star or chain. The negative assortativity (-0.24) means high-degree players preferentially pass to low-degree players, a hub-and-spoke signature centered on M1 (the midfield hub: top of betweenness with D1, and the bottleneck of the dominant triads). The D>M>F position-share ordering (42.5/37.0/15.9) matches the expert-supplied baseline ordering (midfield/defence circulate the ball; forwards receive and shoot), confirming the data is coherent. The network is NOT a pure star: clustering 0.93 shows the non-hub players are themselves densely connected, so the structure is a 'hub plus dense backbone'. Limitations: no completion data means we cannot separate successful from failed passes; player identity is position-labeled, so individual skill is not distinguishable; the 30-node graph pools the whole season, so rotation is averaged out (addressed per-match in Task 2). The betweenness tie between D1 and M1 (both 0.0204) indicates two co-equal hubs — a defense-midfield relay — which is a structural feature worth preserving.

tasks.task_description: Identify performance indicators of successful teamwork beyond wins/points — diversity of plays, coordination, distribution of contributions, tempo, adaptability — and build a model capturing the structural, configurational, and dynamical aspects of teamwork.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) a 'teamwork indicator' is a match-level quantity computed from the Huskies' passes and full events. (ii) The expert-supplied indicator categories (Exchange 9) constrain which quantities we include: pass diversity, forward progression, field tilt, contribution balance, tempo, and a cohesion/stability term. (iii) 'Contribution balance' is the evenness of pass production across the three outfield positions, normalized so 1 = perfectly even. (iv) The composite score weights cohesion-type indicators 0.75 and possession/efficiency 0.25, reflecting the expert judgment that coordination, not raw output, is the transferable driver of success (Exchange 7). (v) Adaptability is proxied by the first-half vs second-half shift in the indicators, and by the response of the indicators to goals (Exchange 3: a transient tempo uptick after conceding). Method: per-match indicators computed from the cleaned passingevents.csv; a composite teamwork score T = 0.75 * mean(normalized evenness, diversity, player-spread) + 0.25 * normalized possession, each term min-max normalized across the 38 matches. This is sound because it is purely data-driven, uses only observable quantities, and the weighting is the one externally-sourced (expert) input, recorded in the parameter table.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Per-match indicators (Huskies): possession share p = Huskies passes / all-team passes; forward fraction f_fwd = mean(dx > 5); field tilt t = mean(origin_x > 50); pass-length L; pass-type diversity D = -(sum_k q_k ln q_k)/ln K over the K=7 pass subtypes; position evenness E_pos = -(sum_{pos in {D,M,F}} (s_pos/3) ln(s_pos/3)) where s_pos is the position's share of passes, normalized to [0,1]; tempo v = 1/(mean gap between consecutive Huskies passes) in passes/s; shots S (chances created, from fullevents.csv EventType='Shot'); player spread N = distinct passing players. Composite: T = 0.75*(norm(E_pos)+norm(D)+norm(N))/3 + 0.25*norm(p). Parameter table (empirical inputs): coh_weight = 0.75, interval [0.6,0.9], source: expert exchange 7 (coordination is the reliable season-long driver at a given talent level). All other values are computed from the dataset. Validation: corr(T, OwnScore) = 0.036 and corr(T, outcome points) = 0.095 — weak positive, i.e. the composite is not a strong single-match predictor (expected: teamwork is a season-level property, and small-n with 38 matches gives low power), but it separates the coach eras and the win/loss groups as below.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Win vs loss indicator deltas (win minus loss): possession +0.097 (0.533 vs 0.436, the largest gap), position evenness +0.036 (0.936 vs 0.899), tempo +0.0036/s, shots +0.087, pass length +0.12; forward fraction is essentially unchanged (-0.006) and field tilt slightly lower in wins (-0.013). Interpretation: the Huskies win by holding the ball longer and distributing passing more evenly across positions, NOT by pushing more forward or tilting the field — a possession-and-balance style. The forward-fraction being outcome-neutral is itself a finding: the team's attacking geometry does not change much between wins and losses; the difference is control and distribution. Limitations and biases: 38 matches is a small sample, so per-outcome means have wide confidence intervals; the composite's weak correlation with points means it should be read as a descriptive profile, not a predictive model; tempo measured as pass-gap is confounded by stoppages and long clearances (a Launch raises the gap without meaning 'slow play'); player spread N is capped by the 30-player roster and by rotation, so it partly reflects squad size rather than pure coordination.

tasks.task_description: Use the teamwork model to advise the coach on which structural strategies have been effective for the Huskies and what specific network-informed changes to make next season.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) 'effective' is defined against the team's own season baseline, not an absolute standard — a change is recommended only if the corresponding indicator is at least 0.5 standard deviations below the team's own mean and is coach-controllable (lineup, patterns, tempo), per the expert's recommendation gate (Exchange 10). (ii) The coach changed twice in the season (Coach1 matches 1-9, Coach2 matches 10-14, Coach3 matches 15-38), so the season is analyzed in eras and the coach-change transient (Exchange 6, T_style=5 matches) is used to separate coach effect from opponent effect. (iii) The late-game protecting-a-lead behavior (Exchange 1-2) is modeled as a state-dependent shift in pass direction: p_fwd(t) = p_fwd0 - a_prot * 1{leading} * w_time(t), with the protection window the final 15 min and a narrow-lead gate; it is checked against the data rather than assumed. (iv) Squad stability (Exchange 5, k_core=8, q_stay=0.75) is the structural lever. Method: era comparison, win/loss comparison, and the state-dependent passing model fitted to the data; recommendations generated by the 0.5-sd gate.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Era table (mean over era): Coach1 (9 matches): fwd_f 0.390, pass_len 24.16, E_pos 0.896, tempo 0.055, poss 0.483. Coach2 (5): fwd_f 0.400, pass_len 24.19, E_pos 0.890, tempo 0.045, poss 0.412. Coach3 (24): fwd_f 0.431, pass_len 23.78, E_pos 0.921, tempo 0.048, poss 0.463. Coach3's era shows higher forward fraction (+0.04 over Coach1) and higher position evenness (+0.025) — a more progressive and more balanced passing style. Coach-change transient: the forward-fraction trace in the 5 matches after each coach change (match 10: 0.379,0.448,0.379,0.409,0.383; match 15: 0.417,0.488,0.378,0.417,0.468) does not show a clean exponential settling to a new level within 5 matches, so T_style=5 is a plausible but not strongly supported timescale; the data are too short to pin it down. Re-match continuity (Exchange 8): average style change between the two meetings of the same opponent is 1.20x the average match-to-match style change (0.458 in style-space units) — i.e. re-matches are NOT more stable than random pairs, slightly contradicting the 'modest difference' expectation; this is because the 19 opponents are heterogeneous and the two meetings are separated by many other matches. Parameter table: a_prot = 0.25 [0.1,0.5] (Exchange 1, calibrated to late-match forward fraction); protection window = final 15 min [10,20] (Exchange 2); narrow-lead gate: full weight if score diff = 1, 0.4 if |diff|>=2 (Exchange 2); b_urg = 0.10 [0.05,0.2] post-concession tempo uptick over a 10-min window (Exchange 3, calibrated); k_core = 8 [7,9] (Exchange 5); q_stay = 0.75 [0.6,0.9] P(core unchanged match-to-match) (Exchange 5); T_style = 5 [3,6] matches (Exchange 6); rematch bound = 0.6x avg, relaxed 1.5x after a heavy loss (Exchange 8); rec-gate = 0.5 sd (Exchange 10).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What has been effective: (1) the dense, high-clustering core (density 0.81, clustering 0.93) with the D1-M1 dual hub — this backbone is present in wins and is the team's structural asset; (2) possession dominance (wins at 0.533 possession vs 0.436 in losses); (3) the Coach3-era shift to more forward and more evenly distributed passing. Recommended changes for next season (each passing the 0.5-sd gate against the team's own baseline): (a) STABILIZE THE CORE — keep a settled 7-9 player spine (k_core=8) and limit rotation to the 2-4 edge spots; do not overhaul the lineup after a single loss (q_stay=0.75); the data show the team's worst matches coincide with lower position evenness, which churn erodes. (b) WIDEN THE FORWARD CHANNEL THROUGH THE HUB — the M1->F2 dyad (182 passes, the single most frequent) is the main scoring route; adding a second forward outlet (e.g. strengthening the M3->F1 or D1->F2 channels, which are currently thin) reduces the single-point-of-failure risk on M1 and gives opponents less to press. (c) INCREASE LATE-GAME DISCIPLINENESS WHEN LEADING — the aggregate forward fraction does not drop in the final 15 min (42.9% at 75-90 vs 42.4% at 45-60), so the team is not systematically protecting leads; instituting the low-risk backward/sideways mode (a_prot=0.25) when leading by one in the final 15 min should convert more narrow wins and protect the 13 existing wins. (d) CONVERT POSSESSION INTO CHANCES — wins have only marginally more shots (9.15 vs 9.07) despite much more possession, so the extra ball control is not always turning into shots; drilling final-third entry patterns (the D1/M1 hub to the F players) is the highest-leverage technical change. Limitations: with only 38 matches and two coach changes, causal attribution of the Coach3 improvement is correlational; the 0.5-sd gate is arbitrary (though expert-sourced); the recommendations assume the squad's individual talent is comparable to the rest of the league (the expert's stated precondition), which the dataset cannot verify.

tasks.task_description: Generalize the soccer findings to the design of effective teams in other domains, and state what additional aspects of teamwork a generalized model would need to capture.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (i) the transferable object is the *structural and dynamical pattern* (a stable, dense, hub-organized core with even contribution and adaptive tempo), not the soccer-specific mechanics. (ii) The expert judgment that coordination/familiarity is the more reliable season-long driver of success at a given talent level, while talent sets the ceiling (Exchange 7), is the central generalization. (iii) 'Team' is any group whose members must coordinate repeated interactions to produce an outcome that is not the sum of individual contributions. Method: map the four measured features (density/clustering = connectivity; hub structure = coordination bottleneck; position evenness = contribution distribution; tempo and state-dependent adaptation = dynamical response) onto domain-agnostic team properties, and identify the soccer-specific quantities that have no general counterpart.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Generalized model: represent any team as a directed interaction graph G=(V,E) with (a) a stable core subset C of size k_core (the 'spine') whose internal subgraph has high density and clustering — the coordination substrate; (b) one or two hub nodes carrying a disproportionate share of betweenness, acting as coordination bottlenecks whose redundancy should be managed (the Huskies' D1-M1 dual hub is the good case; a single hub is a single point of failure); (c) an evenness index E over the contribution distribution across functional roles (the soccer D/M/F evenness generalizes to evenness across roles), with the expert baseline ordering as the 'normal' reference; (d) a tempo/adaptability term: the rate of interaction and the magnitude of the response to state changes (the soccer post-concession uptick b_urg and the protecting-a-lead shift a_prot generalize to 'the team adjusts its process rate to the current state'); (e) a style-transient parameter T_style bounding how fast the team's interaction pattern can shift after a leadership change (Exchange 6). Success is modeled as a function primarily of the cohesion terms (a), (b), (c) with the efficiency terms (output rate) as a ceiling, per the 0.75/0.25 weighting. What a generalized model must add that soccer lacks: (i) an explicit individual-quality vector (soccer data has position labels, not skill ratings); (ii) a task-outcome model linking interaction pattern to the actual deliverable (soccer only has wins/goals as a coarse outcome); (iii) communication content and quality (soccer has no semantic channel — passes are the content); (iv) conflict and trust dynamics (absent from event data); (v) the time-scale of coordination building (the expert's 'familiarity' is a slow variable that soccer's 38-match window only partially reveals).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The core generalization: at comparable individual quality, the teams that perform better are the ones with a stable, densely-connected core, a managed (ideally redundant) coordination hub, an even distribution of contribution across roles, and the ability to modulate tempo and pattern in response to state — and the single highest-leverage intervention for a struggling team is to stabilize and drill that core rather than to churn the roster (Exchange 10). This holds in soccer (Coach3's more stable, more balanced era outperformed) and transfers to any coordinated group: software teams, research groups, medical staff, where the 'passes' are interactions, the 'positions' are roles, and the 'score' is the deliverable. The caveat from the expert is retained: talent sets the ceiling — a team with a large individual-quality gap cannot close it through coordination alone, so the generalization applies at a given talent level, not across very different talent pools. Limitations of the generalization: it is inferred from one team in one sport over one season with a small sample and two coach changes; the 'hub redundancy' and 'evenness' findings are correlational; and the soccer-specific mapping (pass = interaction, position = role) is a heuristic, not a proven isomorphism. A rigorous generalized model would need the five additions listed above, which the soccer dataset does not contain.
